Photocatalytic Chemoselective Cyclic Oxysulfonylation of 2,3-
Allenoic Acids
Yaqi Shi, Chunling Fu, Jian Zheng,* and Shengming Ma*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 5182−5186
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: Photoinduced cyclization of 2,3-allenoic acids with
sulfonyl chloride providing an efficient synthesis of 4-sulfonylated
furan-2(5H)-ones under mild reaction conditions has been
achieved. The reaction enjoys a high chemoselectivity and tolerates
a wide range of functional groups. The catalytic cycle has been
validated through control experiments, cyclic voltammetry studies,
and Stern−Volmer quenching studies.
4-Sulfonylated furan-2(5H)-ones are widely found in natural
products and bioactive molecules (Scheme 1a).
1,2
Therefore,
methods to access this sort of skeleton are of great significance.
The traditional pathway to afford these compounds is the
oxidation of 2(5H)-furanonyl thioethers in the presence of
stoichiometric amounts of strong oxidants (Scheme 1b).
3
On
the other hand, allenoic acids have been widely employed to
synthesize furan-2(5H)-one derivatives due to their high
reactivity.
4
In 2019, Wu and co-workers disclosed the
Cu(OAc)
2
-catalyzed cyclization of 2,3-allenoic acids with
aryldiazonium tetrafluoroborates with 1.5 equiv of Na
2
S
2
O
5
or 1.0 equiv of DABCO·(SO
2
)
2
as the SO
2
source at 60 °C
(Scheme 1c-1).
5
Recently, this transformation was also realized
with cyclobutanone oxime ester under FeCl
2
catalysis with 2.0
equiv of K
2
S
2
O
5
as the SO
2
source at 60 °C (Scheme 1c-2).
6
The direct sulfonylation of 2,3-allenoic acids with readily
available sulfonyl chloride
7
should be an atom economic
strategy, however, has never been realized. The challenge is
how to efficiently break the S(O
2
)−Cl bond, control the
regioselectivity referring to the two C�C bonds in allene, and
control the stereoselectivity required for the cyclization.
Herein, we realize such a reaction via a photocatalytic strategy
at room temperature affording 4-sulfonylated furan-2(5H)-
ones (Scheme 1d).
We began our studies with the coupling reaction of 4-
phenyl-2-propyl-2,3-butadienoic acid 1a and benzenesulfonyl
chloride 2a (2.0 equiv). First of all, the cyclization was tried
under the traditional electrophilic cyclization conditions
(Scheme 2);
8
however, the expected cyclization product, 4-
sulfonylated furan-2(5H)-one 3aa, was not observed with the
starting materials untouched.

Interestingly, under visible-light irradiation, the desired
product, 5-phenyl-4-(phenylsulfonyl)-3-propylfuran-2(5H)-
one (3aa) was formed in 58% with 10% chlorosulfonylation
product (Z)-4aa as a byproduct when 4CzIPN was employed
as the photocatalyst (Table S1, entry 1; for details, see the
Supporting Information), indicating that the stereoselectivity is
indeed an issue. After testing a series of photocatalysts,
Ir(ppy)
2
(dtbbpy)PF
6
was found to offer 3aa in an optimal
yield of 76% with 16% chlorosulfonylation product (Z)-4aa
(Table S1, entries 2−5). Solvent screening indicates that DCM
was still the best (Table S1, entries 6−8). The reaction may be
conducted with 1.0 equiv of 2a with a slightly higher
chemoselectivity (Table S1, entry 5 vs entry 9). Furthermore,
it was found that, when the reaction was conducted with a
concentration of 0.03 M, the yield of 3aa was 82% with 9%
yield of (Z)-4aa (Table S1, entry 10). Subsequently, we also
screened some additives such as TsOH·H
2
O, AcOH, and
NaOAc (Table S1, entries 12−14), and TsOH·H
2
O delivered
the best result. Control experiments revealed that both the
light and the photocatalyst were essential for the trans-
formation (Table S1, entries 15 and 16). Running the reaction
on 1.0 mmol scale at 0.05 M has been defined as the optimal
conditions, affording 3aa in 69% yield with a remarkable
selectivity of 3aa/(Z)-4aa (Table S1, entry 18). Furthermore,
the reaction with 427-nm blue LEDs is still the optimal choice
after the light source test (Table S1, entries 19−21). The
structure of byproduct (Z)-4aa was further confirmed by (Z)-
4le being esterificated to afford (Z)-10le, which has been
clearly identified by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (CCDC
No. 2127599; for details, see page S35 in the Supporting
Information).
The scope of 2,3-allenoic acids and sulfonyl chlorides has
been explored, as shown in Table 1. The cyclization reaction of
2,3-allenoic acid 1a with benzenesulfonyl chloride 2a afforded
the corresponding product 3aa in 63% yield with a selectivity
of 92/8 for 3aa/(Z)-4aa. When the reaction was conducted in
air, the target product 3aa was not observed, with 7% recovery
of 1a. The structure of 3aa was further confirmed by X-ray

analysis. Different electron-withdrawing-group-substituted 4-
aryl 2,3-allenoic acids 1b−1g performed well under the
standard conditions, affording the corresponding products
3ba−3ga in good yields. When 2,3-allenoic acid with the
methylthio-substituted aryl moiety 1h was applied, the desired
product 3ha was obtained in 43% yield. Moreover, 2,3-allenoic
acids bearing a methoxy group at the para-, meta-, and ortho-
position of the 4-aryl group all afforded the desired products
3ia−3ka in moderate yields. It is worth mentioning that 46%,
52%, and 28% of cycloisomerization products 5h, 5i, and 5k
were generated for para-SMe 1h, para-OMe 1i, and ortho-
OMe 1k, respectively.
Furthermore, the n-propyl group in 1a could be replaced
with a methyl group to provide 3la in 51% yield. However, 4-
methyl-substituted 2,3-allenoic acid 1m afforded the desired
product 3ma in a low yield of 15%. When R
2
= 2° alkyl group,
i.e., 2,3-allenoic acid 1n, the reaction could also afford desired
product 3na in 43% yield. It should be noted that
tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoic acid 1o afforded the desired
product 3oa in 13% yield with 75% cycloisomerization product
5o. With regard to sulfonyl chlorides, the substrates tethered
with various synthetically versatile functional groups, such as F,
Cl, Br, CF
3
, Me, and OMe, all afford the corresponding
products 3ab−3ai in moderate yields. Thienyl sulfonyl
chloride 2j also delivered product 3aj in 30% yield. However,
the cyclopropylsulfonyl chloride 2k afforded the corresponding
product 3ak in a low yield of 12% with 6% cycloisomerization
product 5a. And n-propylsulfonyl chloride 2l afforded the
desired product 3al in only 15% yield with 16% of
cycloisomerization product 5a. The reactions of 1a with 1-
naphthalenesulfonyl chloride 2m, dimethylamino sulfonyl
chloride 2n, or D(+)-10-camphorsulfonyl chloride 2o all failed
to afford 3am, 3an, or 3ao under the standard conditions (for
details, see pages S42−S44 in the Supporting Information).
A gram-scale reaction was conducted under the standard
reaction conditions, affording 3aa in 57% yield with a
selectivity of 91/9 for 3aa/(Z)-4aa. In the presence of
LiOAc·2H
2
O, the γ-position of 3aa could be easily oxidized
to give γ-hydroxylated product 6 in 54% yield under an O
2
atmosphere. Deprotonation and subsequent acetylation with
Ac
2
O afforded sulfonylated furan 7. Similarly, an O−P bond
could be formed when 3aa was treated with NaHMDS and
subsequent phosphorylation with ClP(O)(OPh)
2
to offer 8 in
82% yield (Scheme 3).
8b,9
To gain insight into the mechanism, control experiments
were conducted. First, when the reaction of 1a with PhSO
2
Cl
was performed in the presence of 1,1-diphenylethylene (2.0
equiv) under the standard conditions, the formation of 3aa was
totally suppressed and the sulfonylation product of 1,1-
diphenyl-2-benzenesulfonylethylene 9 was produced, indicat-
ing the presence of sulfonyl radical in this transformation
(Scheme 4a). When the byproduct chlorosulfonylation
product (Z)-4aa was submitted to the standard conditions,
desired product 3aa was also observed in 19% yield with 58%
recovery of (Z)-4aa (Scheme 4b). Cyclic voltammetry
experiments confirmed that both 4-phenyl-2,3-allenoic acid

However, Stern−Volmer quenching studies showed that 2a or
2a/TsOH·H
2
O could quench excited photocatalyst *Ir-
(ppy)
2
(dtbbpy)PF
6
more efficiently than 1a. This result
indicated that 2a would be the exact quencher of the excited
photocatalyst in the reaction. Furthermore, 2l, 2k, and 2j were
all demonstrated to display a lower quenching efficiency with
the excited photocatalyst, compared with that of 2a (Scheme
4d).
Based on these experimental data, a possible mechanism is
depicted below using 1a and 2a as the model substrates
(Scheme 5). The excited photocatalyst *[Ir]
III
could be
quenched with 2a to generate [Ir]
IV
and a benzenesulfonyl
radical, which would react with allenoic acid 1a to form radical
anti-Int I as the major intermediate and its stereoisomer syn-
Int I as the minor intermediate. Subsequent oxidation of
radical intermediates, anti-Int I and syn-Int I, with [Ir]
IV
species would afford ground-state photocatalyst [Ir]
III
and
cationic allylic intermediates, anti-Int II or syn-Int II, via a SET
process. 3aa was generated from anti-Int II by intramolecular
nucleophilic substitution. Meanwhile, syn-Int II could be
trapped with Cl
−
to form noncyclized chlorosulfonylation
product (Z)-4aa. When the phenyl group in 1a was replaced
with a methyl group, there is no benzyl effect; thus, the
reaction of 1m gave a poor yield of 3ma (Table 1). The
reactions of 1a with 2j, 2k, and 2l afforded the desired
products 3aj, 3ak, and 3al in poor yields (Table 1), probably
because these compounds quenched the excited photocatalyst
in a mismatched rate (Scheme 4d). It should be noted that
(Z)-4aa could be converted to the target molecule 3aa at a
slow rate.
In summary, a photocatalyzed cyclic oxysulfonylation
reaction of 2,3-allenoic acids with sulfonyl chlorides has been
developed. This protocol enables to prepare the sulfonylated
furan-2(5H)-ones with a high chemoselectivity and a decent
functional group tolerance under mild conditions. The
synthetic application has been proven via versatile trans-
formations of the target molecules. Radical trapping experi-
ments and cyclic voltammetry experiments unveiled that
sulfonyl radical generated via light-induced SET process were
involved via the reductive quenching cycle. In addition, cyclic
voltammetry experiments and Stern−Volmer quenching
